articles.title: Kade Anderson earns first win in Mariners 3-2 win over Rangers
articles.summary: Kade Anderson earns win, Cole Young comes up with big hit, Lazaro Montes doubles in Mariners’ youth movement win
articles.body:
It's not been the easiest start to a career for Kade Anderson, who came into today's game with a loss and two no decisions on the season, and most recently off a four-run outing against the Athletics he called "unacceptable" and not "holding up to the standard" expected by both himself and his teammates. Much has been made of Anderson not facing hitters three times through the order, something that wasn't really an issue as he was mowing hitters down in Double-A but has called into question his future as a big-league starter. Today, Anderson calmly navigated through a Rangers lineup that hung double-digit runs on Mariners pitching last night, working through the sixth inning for the first time as a big-leaguer – and something he did just four times at Double-A – and earning his first MLB win.

"This is just the beginning of – and also this is the standard that I set myself to," said Anderson postgame. "I think pitching is just setting a standard every time you go out there and learning from each individual outing, picking up some things you want to take back [to the next outing] and keep learning with it."

Anderson worked around some traffic in the first inning, giving up a couple of two-out base hits but getting a soft flyout from Wyatt Langford , first-pitch swinging, to end the threat. Those two base hits each came in two-strike counts, one on a fastball that was too nicely located for a 1-2 count and one on a changeup that stayed high to Brandon Nimmo , highlighting the need for Anderson to develop an out pitch that works at this level. He was able to use the curveball to that effect on a nice swinging strikeout of Corey Seager in the first. Check out the sick movement on this curveball:

The only mark on Anderson was he did allow some hard contact – seven balls hit over 100 mph exit velocity, although he did get the Rangers to pound that hard contact into the ground half the time. Jake Burger in particular hit Anderson hard, with a lineout in the fourth that was the hardest-hit ball of the game at 109 mph; he got to Anderson in the second with a leadoff solo homer, taking advantage of a 2-1 count (which probably should have been 1-2 if Cal had challenged the first pitch of the at-bat). But Anderson didn't let it shake him and battled back to get his next three outs to cap the damage there.

What Anderson did particularly well in this game was make in-game adjustments; after Burger got to him in the first, despite the hard-hit ball in the fourth, there was no chance of that ball going out as Anderson executed a changeup that Burger got under. He then capped his day by striking Burger out on the changeup to end the sixth, getting him swinging over it this time.

"Cal came out and said something," said Anderson. "I'm not gonna tell you what he said, but it meant a lot. And he holds me to that standard as well. That's why he's so good. Him holding me to that standard really has helped me continue to adjust to this. What he said just kind of clicked, and that's the standard I hold myself to now."

"To me he looked like he was almost getting stronger as the game went on," said manager Dan Wilson postgame, apparently not privy to what Cal said, either, "which is always a good sign. His confidence continued to grow there throughout the game." Wilson pointed to Anderson's secondaries, in particular, as buoying him along, noting that he was able to get the slider down more as the game progressed.

"I would say that the in-game adjustment today, it just felt different for whatever reason," said Anderson. "It kind of felt like I was back out there pitching again. And it shouldn't have taken me this long to get there. But once again, that's the standard."

The Mariners were able to tie up the game against Rangers starter Cody Bradford in the bottom of the second. Cal Raleigh became the Mariners' first baserunner in the second inning, extending his on-base streak to 11 games, thanks to a savvy challenge on a called strike three that turned a punchout into a walk. However, the Mariners were quickly in a position of needing a clutch two-out knock after Julio Rodríguez punched out on three pitches, and Josh Naylor popped out after burning a challenge on an obvious strike. Enter the much-maligned Taylor Ward , making a start with a lefty on the mound today for Texas, who came up with said clutch hit:

This makes me, personally, very happy. Another happy-making thing: Cal Raleigh is in scoring position there because he took it aggressively on Naylor's popout, which forced the catcher to dive at the wall for the ball. Heads-up baserunning for Cal and a gold star for him.

Anderson again had to navigate around some traffic in the third, leaving a curveball on the plate for Seager, who singled, and then following that up with a walk to Justin Foscue , unable to get a big-league hitter to expand away the same way he might have gotten a minor-leaguer to do. But he got a weak ground ball from Nimmo, first-pitch swinging on a slider, and then went full count with Langford before striking him out swinging on a slider.

Anderson then hung a clean fourth inning, his first of the day, and the Mariners rewarded him with some two-out offense in the bottom of the inning: Josh Naylor reached on what should have been an inning-ending groundout to Seager that instead took a funny hop, and then Taylor Ward made that mistake count by working a walk, increasing my happiness meter all the way into the double digits. Cole Young then continued what's been a hot September for him, demolishing this offensively bad fastball from Bradford for a two-run double that missed being a homer by about one Cole Young.

Your browser does not support the video tag. Download the video .

After a dismal August, Young has roared back in the early days of September. He's increased his wRC+ from 53 all the way to 132.

"I feel like sometimes in August, you just get caught up and try to do too much or try to come through in a situation, and put pressure on that," said Young, who is in his second (2nd) big-league August. "But I feel like going into this month, I'm just trying to trust my routine, trust the process, and just try to hit the ball hard somewhere, and if it gets caught, it gets caught. But just trusting my abilities and putting the ball in play."

"I'm always just trying to simplify things, and I feel like it's easy to get caught up in certain results and all of that stuff. So it's just big for me to stay simple and hit the ball hard somewhere and not really worry about what the outcome is, moreso the process behind it and just trusting that."

Then it was time for Anderson to face his běte noire: the third time through the order. Before that even started, though, he gave up a leadoff single in the fifth to nine-hole hitter Cody Freeman , but then was able to execute a well-located four-seamer to leadoff man Ezequiel Duran for a weak flyout, and wound up facing the minimum after getting Seager to ground into a 4-3 double play on a changeup. He couldn't post a clean inning in the sixth, either, giving up a one-out first-pitch single to Nimmo on a four-seamer that wound up in the middle of the plate, but came back to strike out Langford for the second time on the day – and making him burn Texas's lone remaining challenge in doing so – on a nasty slider and then striking out Burger on the aforementioned changeup to close up a strong day of work for the youngster.

Anderson was pumping 95s in his final inning, with his slider pushing up to 90, making me think he was deliberately emptying the tank, perhaps having been told his day was done. But according to Anderson, this wasn't the case.

"It was more of a mentality, like, attacking guys. It felt like when I made that adjustment, my velo shot up, I was throwing things more aggressively in the zone. It felt like at some points I was trying to over-locate like throwing something by a dude, and I think that was the biggest game changer."

"That's another adjustment I've had throughout my starts: stop thinking it's the last inning. It's more, it's just another inning. I think that's gotten me over the hump to where I'm not trying to empty the tank necessarily, just treat it like another inning and stop trying to think like the finish line is near."

While I was hoping to see Kade get a chance to face the bottom of the order and make a full turn through all three times, Dan Wilson opted to lift his young starter while he had the lead and end his day on a positive note. Unfortunately, this gave the Mariners bullpen three innings to cover, starting with Seranthony Dominguez . Dominguez led off with a walk to pinch-hitter Joc Pederson on five pitches, four of which were not competitive misses, but got Elias Díaz whiffing after 98. The Rangers continued to empty their bench of lefties with Anderson out of the game, pinch-hitting Evan Carter , who flew out to left. That turned the lineup over for Duran, who grounded out softly on a splitter to quell the threat.

The Mariners had a chance to expand their lead in the bottom of the seventh, with pinch-hitter Laz Montes coming up with a two-out parachute hustle double followed by a J.P. Crawford walk, but Randy Arozarena grounded out to end the threat, giving Gabe Speier the same slender lead Dominguez and Anderson had been gifted. Speier immediately gave up one of those runs on a first-pitch middle-middle sinker to Seager, who yanked it just far enough over the wall in left for an opposite-field homer. So it goes. Speier was able to recover and get his next three outs, but the already-narrow-lead was even narrower.

The offense couldn't add on in the bottom of the inning – despite an unfortunately rare-feeling Julio single – giving Andrés Muñoz, he of the Funko Pop giveaway today, the thinnest of margins. I'm so sick of coming up with adjective for "little," Mariners offense. Muñoz wobbled out of the gate, walking leadoff hitter Burger on five pitches and prompting a mound visit. After that, though, Muñoz buckled down. Joc Pederson grounded out weakly on a changeup, but it was as good as a bunt, moving pinch-runner Cam Cauley into second. The Rangers went again to their bench for pinch-hitter Nicky Lopez , who was helpless against Muñoz, flailing after 101.2 and then two changeups, each at 94 (aka, as fast as starter Kade Anderson's fastball). Evan Carter was the Rangers' last hope, but he went the same way as Lopez: on three pitches, fouling off 101, then the changeup at 94, and then swinging after an absolutely diabolical changeup at 95. I don't know why this pitch works and frankly, I don't think it's my place to.

It stinks to be looking for silver linings in a season that had such hope and promise, but if you're collecting little glimmers of hope to store away like seeds for the long coming winter, this game had plenty to offer: Cole Young emerging from his August torpor; Lazaro Montes coming up with a pinch-hit hustle double; Andrés Muñoz with a new weapon that can get him out of spirals and also obliterate batters' souls; and Kade Anderson looking like the pitcher he was in the minors. That's a lot to dream on, going forward.

articles.title: Jalen Hurts, Sean Mannion face new communication test in Week 1
articles.summary: Jalen Hurts will communicate with Sean Mannion by phone as the Eagles’ new coordinator calls plays from the booth in Week 1
articles.body:
Jalen Hurts will experience another change Sunday when Sean Mannion calls plays from the coaches' booth during the Philadelphia Eagles' season opener against the Washington Commanders . Hurts said this will be the first time in his NFL career that his primary play caller has worked from the booth instead of the sideline. That physical separation creates an adjustment as Philadelphia begins implementing its new offense under Mannion.

"There is a wall there," Hurts said, according to John Clark of NBC Sports Philadelphia .

Instead of speaking directly with Mannion on the sideline, Hurts will communicate by telephone between possessions and explain what he is seeing from Washington's defense. The quarterback can still speak face-to-face with quarterbacks coach Alex Tanney and other offensive assistants working at field level.

Mannion experimented with calling plays from the sideline and booth during the preseason before settling on the elevated position. The booth should provide a clearer view of defensive formations, coverage rotations and potential adjustments. The challenge will be developing an efficient communication process with Hurts during the limited time between possessions.

Hurts acknowledged that the offense remains in transition and said he does not know exactly what it will look like. Its identity could change weekly based on opponents, matchups and the concepts Mannion chooses to emphasize.

Philadelphia's offensive players have revealed little about what will be unveiled Sunday, but they have consistently described the system as an ongoing process. Hurts and Mannion built their foundation during offseason workouts, training camp, and preseason practices. Their most meaningful chemistry, however, can only develop through regular-season experience.

That process begins against Washington, with Mannion watching from above and Hurts responsible for bringing their shared vision to life on the field.

articles.title: Cowboys have a pretty 'cool' way of tracking the heat as they settle for indoor practices
articles.summary: The Dallas Cowboys are hiding from the Texas heat out of necessity, practicing inside on artificial turf rather than outside on grass as they would prefer no...
articles.body:
FRISCO, Texas (AP) — The Dallas Cowboys are hiding from the Texas heat out of necessity, practicing inside on artificial turf rather than outside on grass as they would prefer now that the regular-season routine is finally here.

Brian Schottenheimer isn't sure how much a brutal summer that's still on full blast in September will have to ease up for the Cowboys to get back outside. The coach has seen an interesting way of finding the answer.

"It's more of the humidity and what we're doing with the sweating. And we do all the sweat testing," Schottenheimer said. "We've got these cool urinals. I don't know how much they cost, but they must be expensive. It tells you whatever your urination levels are. It's crazy."

The Dallas area hasn't had measurable rainfall in nearly two months. Wednesday was the eighth day of September with a triple-digit high temperature, tying a record.

The Cowboys have their last full practice of the week Thursday, three days before the season opener at the New York Giants . The forecast calls for temperatures in the 90s Fahrenheit and a chance for rain, but Schottenheimer said the team was "probably" headed for another day inside.

The indoor facility at Cowboys headquarters is actually a 12,000-seat stadium that is used for high school games. The grass field is a short walk away, between the locker room and the dining room.

When Dallas practices inside, brief periods for different position groups sometimes move outside. But if they do, those sessions don't last long.

Schottenheimer held two shorter outdoor practices last week, but both started at 8 a.m. The regular practice time is early afternoon, but the triple-digit heat index at that time has been nearly constant for weeks. It could linger into the second half of September.

"I think the way the schedule's built this year for the first couple games, we're not going to be able to have much of a routine," Schottenheimer said. "So that's why the whole live in the moment, win the day, I think matters. If I felt like the only way for us to get ready to perform well in this game was to go outside, I can promise you we'd go outside."

Strange as it may sound, Schottenheimer would put the aforementioned urinals in the sports science category. He says science is driving the decision to practice inside or outside.

"We're just trying to do what we can to avoid the heat," Schottenheimer said. "We don't play in the heat. So right now we're just trying to do our best to get on the grass for certain things and then be inside for certain things. And right now we just feel we can get better work done inside."

That's what some of the, uh, measurables are saying.

articles.title: Red Sox's Plan for Garrett Crochet Couldn't be Better, and Here's Why
articles.summary: The Red Sox are making a verey smart decision with their ace.
articles.body:
With the postseason nearly here for the Boston Red Sox , the bigger focus isn't even on who they're going to play or how things might unfold in the wild card, but which players they're going to get back.

The Red Sox still have multiple players out with injuries, along with guys who just recently returned. Whether it's Roman Anthony , Trevor Story , or Garrett Crochet , there are plenty of questions that have to be answered about three of the better players on the roster. Anthony looks fine, Story will eventually get going, but Crochet still hasn't returned.

While there's an expectation that Crochet could return sometime in the near future, there's also a known reality that he isn't going to be a starter.

The Red Sox are being very smart with this decision by not rushing him back and asking him to throw too many innings, as they recognize that keeping Crochet healthy in the long term is much more important than whatever happens in October.

Regarding what his role might look like if he returns, skipper Chad Tracy had a lot to say about possibly being an opener. He also spoke about coming in during the middle of games.

"He'd have plenty of comfort opening if you wanted to go that route," Tracy said, per Jen McCaffrey.

"He pitched out of 'pen. So if you need him to come in the middle innings of a game, a two-inning pocket, I'm sure he'd have comfort doing that too. That's the beauty of it. If he's healthy and ready and he looks like Garrett, there's different things you can do. I hate getting too far ahead of myself. I just want to see him continue to check the boxes he needs to check and as we get closer and it feels like, 'Hey, this is a realistic thing now,' then we can kind of figure out what that is."

The promising part with Crochet, and the reality that the Red Sox need to recognize, is that he's thrown out of the bullpen for most of his career. This isn't a guy who doesn't know how to come in during the back half of a game and get outs, even if he hasn't done it over the past few seasons.

Crochet was one of the best relievers in all of baseball just a few seasons ago. With an electric fastball and elite stuff, he'll be in a spot to come in at any moment. With him and Aroldis Chapman in the backend of a bullpen, the Red Sox will have a major advantage.

That experience should help the Red Sox a lot in the postseason.

articles.title: Richard Sherman to raise the 12th Man Flag against the Patriots

articles.body:
The Seattle Seahawks enjoy the best pregame tradition in all of football. Before every game, the iconic 12th Man Flag is raised in the south end zone by a former Seahawk legend, Seattle sports icon or local celebrity. Now, we know who will be raising the flag on Wednesday night against the New England Patriots , and it is a familiar face:

The face of the Legion of Boom defense, who helped usher in the golden age and won the franchise their first Super Bowl, is on deck to help the team celebrate their second.

Sherman was a Seahawk from 2011-2017 and helped put the Seahawks on the map by giving them a loud, brash brand unseen in the Pacific Northwest before. During his time in Seattle, Sherman was unequestionably the best cornerback in the league. In back to back years, he was the least targeted corner in the NFL and still led the league in interceptions.

Initially, it seemed as if Jody Allen was going to be the flag raiser, as was suggested by the new owner Vinod Khosla. However, Richard Sherman is quite fitting for Wednesday night!

articles.title: SEC not expected to vote on LSU's membership this week, AP source says
articles.summary: The Southeastern Conference is no longer expected to vote on whether to expel LSU from the league on Thursday, a person familiar with the matter said Wednesd...
articles.body:
NEW ORLEANS (AP) — The Southeastern Conference is no longer expected to vote on whether to expel LSU from the league on Thursday, a person familiar with the matter said Wednesday evening.

The person spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because Thursday's meeting — to be held by video conference — is not open to the public and because the SEC has not released a statement on the matter since a federal court filing on Tuesday highlighted the league's intent to vote on LSU's membership.

The dispute between the conference and LSU stems largely from first-year Tigers coach Lane Kiffin's now-abandoned bid to field two players who had signed NFL contracts as undrafted rookies this past offseason.

A hearing scheduled Wednesday in a federal lawsuit the SEC filed against LSU was postponed by a judge in Birmingham, Alabama.

Meanwhile, LSU President Wade Rousse sent a one-page letter, obtained by the AP, to SEC commissioner Greg Sankey stating that the league's claims in its lawsuit against LSU are now moot because Kiffin had complied with a conference ban on rostering players who had previously signed contracts with NFL teams.

Rousse noted that he called Sankey last Friday afternoon and notified him personally that LSU would not be placing tight end Dae'Quan Wright or defensive tackle Zxavian Harris on the Tigers' roster.

Wright had spent part of the past offseason with the Philadelphia Eagles and Cleveland Browns . Harris has spent part of the offseason with the New Orleans Saints . Both also had played for Mississippi when Kiffin was the Rebels' coach.

LSU on Tuesday filled remaining vacancies on its roster with eligible players.

"The roster is now locked for the season," Rousse's letter stated. "LSU complied with SEC rules. This issue is moot."

Rousse also noted that LSU "will not challenge, disrupt or seek to cancel or postpone" Thursday's scheduled meeting — a concern Sankey had raised Tuesday in the SEC's amended federal complaint against LSU.

LSU is a founding member of the SEC, which was formed in 1933. LSU has a host of powerhouse athletics programs and has won three of the SEC's 25 AP national championships in football alone.

Still, the language in the federal lawsuit left little ambiguity about the extent to which the leaders of most SEC universities had become frustrated with LSU — not only because of efforts to recruit former pros to both its football and men's basketball teams.

They also were unhappy about the related court drama that ensued — including a marathon court hearing last week in which Sankey took the stand to insist the league has the right to enforce its own rules.

Sankey said there was consensus among conference leaders that "LSU's continued membership in the conference would be inconsistent with the publicly stated values and principles of the conference and its remaining member institutions," even if LSU doesn't put the former NFL players on its roster.

The SEC has a long-established rule forbidding teams from bringing players with major professional experience onto their rosters. In recent weeks, the conference announced updated enforcement provisions to that rule, stating that the commissioner had the power to suspend coaches, fine universities up to half of a sport's budget and restrict a member university's voting privileges on conference matters.

But last Thursday, a judge in Baton Rouge barred the league from enforcing any rules regarding former pros — a decision celebrated heartily by Louisiana Gov. Jeff Landry and the state attorney general, Liz Murrill, who'd filed a brief in the case on behalf of the athletes.

Murrill called the SEC's lawsuit "legal garbage" shortly after it was filed last week.; The SEC has since listed Murrill as a defendant.

Sankey has stated that SEC presidents are concerned that Rousse and athletic director Verge Ausberry have no "meaningful control" over Kiffin or the football program.

Sankey also stated that "serious harm" had been caused "by the statements and conduct of LSU," and suggested that harm would not be undone simply by LSU renouncing "its intention to roster and play professional players on its football team."

Kiffin's hiring was one of two notable coaching changes at LSU involving the highest revenue-generating college sports: LSU also has brought back Will Wade to coach men's basketball. Wade was fired by previous athletic director Scott Woodward in the wake of an NCAA investigation into improper inducement payments to recruits when such payments were forbidden.

Wade served a suspension from coaching in college before returning in the 2023-24 season with McNeese State. He spent two seasons with the Cowboys and one with North Carolina State before he was brought back to LSU — a move favored by Landry, as well as Rousse, a Landry ally who was McNeese's president when Wade was there.

Wade has sought to sign RJ Luis Jr., a former Big East player of the year with St. John's who spent parts of the 2025 NBA offseason and preseason with the Utah Jazz and Boston Celtics, but never played in a regular-season NBA game.

Luis also has been fighting the NCAA in court in Baton Rouge, where a judge on Aug. 24 issued a preliminary injunction that temporarily blocks the NCAA from punishing LSU if the Tigers play Luis — something that also would violate the SEC rules at the center of the conference's federal lawsuit against LSU.

LSU's football team is now ranked eighth in the Top 25 AP Poll following Saturday's 51-10, season-opening victory over Clemson . The Tigers host Louisiana Tech on Saturday, followed by a much anticipated visit to No. 9 Ole Miss, where Kiffin will face the team he coached a year ago.

articles.title: Girls soccer: Lady Lions post EIAC win against Connersville
articles.summary: The matchup between Rushville and Connersville on the pitch could not be decided in regulation or the two overtime sessions. It took a penalty kick shootout...
articles.body:
The matchup between Rushville and Connersville on the pitch could not be decided in regulation or the two overtime sessions. It took a penalty kick shootout for the Lady Lions to get the 4-2 victory.

Freshman Ava Peggs scored the only goal in regulation for the Lady Lions. The game was tied 1-1 after the 80 minute regulation time. The Lady Lions and Lady Spartans remained tied after two 7-minute overtimes.

In the shootout, Rushville keeper Kalaina Harper only allowed one goal of the five shots to be scored.

Rushville's Anna Beth Chastain, Izzy Simmermon and Annie Buzzard all found the back of the net for the Lady Lions to secure the conference win.

Rushville improves to 5-3 on the season.

The junior varsity Lady Lions also came home with a win 2-1. Keanna Bennett scored both goals for the Lady Lions. Natalie Dora had four saves during the 35-minute JV half.

Saturday, the Lady Lions traveled to Lawrenceburg to face a talented Lady Tigers team. Rushville keeper Kalaina Harper recorded 30 saves. Lawrenceburg posted the 6-0 win.

The Lady Pirates went on the road to Centerville to pick up another win on the season. The Lady Pirates scored three goals in the first half and backed that up with four goals in the second half en route to the 7-2 victory.

Greensburg's Kadence Rich scored four goals. Emma Kennelly found the net for a pair of goals. Kelsey Wentzel added one goal.

Maria Scholle dished out five assists in the game. Rachel Lipps and Alexis Weber both had one assist in the win.

Greensburg's offensive pressure resulted in 31 shots on goal: Scholle 10, Rich eight, Kennelly six, Wentzel three, Lipps two, Weber one and Mackenzie Schwering one.

Greensburg keeper Peyton Powers recorded eight saves. Hadley Meyer added two saves.

The Lady Bulldogs hosted EIAC foe Lawrenceburg on the grass field and split with the Lady Tigers. Batesville won the varsity contest 4-0. Lawrenceburg prevailed in the junior varsity match 3-0.

Four minutes into the varsity game, Batesville's Addie Reding received a pass from Elia Wade and then placed the ball past the keeper and into the corner of the goal.

Wade then got the team's second goal of the night, by running onto a through ball, cut in front of a defender and then placed the ball into the corner of the net. Before the end of the half, Reding scored her second goal of the night. Sydney Britton sent a pass to Reding, who headed the ball into space and then drilled in a shot from the 18-yard box.

Britton was able to score the only goal in the second half, by taking a deep shot from outside the corner of the 18-yard box.

Batesville's defense was stellar. The defensive line of Nora Wiedeman, Savannah Pohlman, Emma Cheeks, Cora Miller, Kenzi Lacey and Bailey Feldmann played a huge role in the shutout. Keeper Brynlie Oesterling recorded her fifth shutout of the season with 16 saves tonight.
